claim: Enzymerhodopsins represent a recently discovered class of rhodopsins which includes histidine kinase rhodopsin, rhodopsin phosphodiesterases, and rhodopsin guanylyl cyclases (RGCs).
source: Enzymerhodopsins represent a recently discovered class of rhodopsins which includes histidine kinase rhodopsin, rhodopsin phosphodiesterases, and rhodopsin guanylyl cyclases (RGCs).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about enzymerhodopsins that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The regulatory influence of the rhodopsin domain on the enzyme activity is only partially understood.
source: The regulatory influence of the rhodopsin domain on the enzyme activity is only partially understood and holds the key for a deeper understanding of intra-molecular signaling pathways.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current understanding based on the state of the field.

claim: The cytosolic N-terminus is involved in structural rearrangements upon photo-activation of CaRGC.
source: we analyzed truncated variants and revealed the involvement of the cytosolic N-terminus in the structural rearrangements upon photo-activation of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental analysis of truncated variants presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substrate binding occurs to the dark-adapted RGC.
source: Our results show substrate binding to the dark-adapted RGC and GC alike and reveal differences between the constructs attributable to the regulatory influence of the rhodopsin on the conformation of the binding pocket.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: The M state is the active state of RGC during cGMP formation.
source: By monitoring the phosphate rearrangement during cGMP and pyrophosphate formation in light-activated RGC, we were able to confirm the M state as the active state of the protein.
evidence: This claim is confirmed by monitoring phosphate rearrangements during catalysis as described in the manuscript.

claim: The ubiquitous intracellular second messenger molecule cGMP is involved in a wide variety of biological functions such as platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, blood pressure, long bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, and oocyte maturation.
source: Throughout most branches of life, the ubiquitous intracellular second messenger molecule cGMP is involved in a wide variety of biological functions such as platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, blood pressure, long bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, and oocyte maturation (Potter, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Potter, 2011.

claim: Enzymerhodopsins enable local control of cGMP and, if modified, cAMP.
source: Since enzymerhodopsins enable local control of cGMP and, if modified, cAMP (Scheib et al., 2018), they usher in a new direction for optogenetics aiming to unravel the details of these signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2018.

claim: The RGC was first discovered in the aquatic fungus Blastocladiella emersonii as the photoreceptor responsible for the phototactic behavior of the fungal zoospores.
source: The RGC was first discovered in the aquatic fungus Blastocladiella emersonii as the photoreceptor responsible for the phototactic behavior of the fungal zoospores (Avelar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Avelar et al., 2014.

claim: In vitro studies confirmed the function of RGC as a photoactivated guanylyl cyclase that is inactive in the dark and fully active when illuminated with green light.
source: In vitro studies confirmed its function as a photoactivated guanylyl cyclase that is inactive in the dark and fully active when illuminated with green light (Scheib et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2015.

claim: The crystal structure of the constitutively active isolated cyclase domain of CaRGC is available.
source: More functional details are available from the orthologous protein of the related fungus Catenaria anguillulae (CaRGC) including the crystal structure of the constitutively active isolated cyclase domain (Scheib et al., 2018; Butryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheib et al., 2018 and Butryn et al., 2020.

claim: CaRGC assembles as a homodimer.
source: The results show the photoreceptor to assemble as a homodimer, with the rhodopsin modules responsible to silence the cyclase activity in darkness.
evidence: This is a statement of results from previous studies on CaRGC.

claim: The rhodopsin modules are responsible to silence the cyclase activity in darkness.
source: The results show the photoreceptor to assemble as a homodimer, with the rhodopsin modules responsible to silence the cyclase activity in darkness.
evidence: This is a statement of results from previous studies on CaRGC.

claim: A number of enzymerhodopsins have been purified and enzymatically and spectroscopically characterized.
source: Meanwhile, a number of enzymerhodopsins have been purified and enzymatically and spectroscopically characterized (Trieu et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2017; Yoshida et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2018; Watari et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies that characterized enzymerhodopsins.

claim: The canonical hepta-helical rhodopsin module is preceded by an additional eighth transmembrane helix (TM0) in enzymerhodopsins.
source: In all of them, the canonical hepta-helical rhodopsin module is preceded by an additional eighth transmembrane helix (TM0), leading to a cytosolic localization of both termini.
evidence: This is a structural feature observed across enzymerhodopsins as stated in the manuscript.

claim: The additional eighth transmembrane helix (TM0) leads to a cytosolic localization of both termini in enzymerhodopsins.
source: In all of them, the canonical hepta-helical rhodopsin module is preceded by an additional eighth transmembrane helix (TM0), leading to a cytosolic localization of both termini.
evidence: This is a structural consequence of the TM0 helix as stated in the manuscript.

claim: No full-length structural model of an enzymerhodopsin is available to date.
source: To date, however, no full-length structural model of an enzymerhodopsin is available, leaving the mechanism of how photoactivation of the rhodopsin regulates enzyme function, including the role of the cytoplasmic N-terminus, unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of structural knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: The crystal structures of the isolated transmembrane and intracellular catalytic domains were solved separately for RPDEs from choanoflagellates.
source: Recently, the crystal structures of the isolated transmembrane and intracellular catalytic domains were solved separately for RPDEs from choanoflagellates, which are already active in the dark and only moderately stimulated under illumination (Lamarche et al., 2017; Ikuta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamarche et al., 2017 and Ikuta et al., 2020.

claim: RPDEs from choanoflagellates are already active in the dark and only moderately stimulated under illumination.
source: Recently, the crystal structures of the isolated transmembrane and intracellular catalytic domains were solved separately for RPDEs from choanoflagellates, which are already active in the dark and only moderately stimulated under illumination (Lamarche et al., 2017; Ikuta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamarche et al., 2017 and Ikuta et al., 2020.

claim: An initial spectroscopic characterization of CaRGC identified three subsequent photocycle intermediates designated as K, L, and M-states.
source: An initial spectroscopic characterization of CaRGC identified three subsequent photocycle intermediates designated as K, L, and M-states according to the nomenclature derived from bacteriorhodopsin as prototypical microbial rhodopsin (Scheib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2018.

claim: The M state of CaRGC decays within a few hundred ms.
source: The M state decays within a few hundred ms, but the K and L states only rest in the sub-µ to µs time range, which makes them unfeasible for investigation by rapid scan FTIR.
evidence: This is a statement about the kinetics of photocycle intermediates based on previous characterization.

claim: The K and L states of CaRGC only rest in the sub-µs to µs time range.
source: The M state decays within a few hundred ms, but the K and L states only rest in the sub-µ to µs time range, which makes them unfeasible for investigation by rapid scan FTIR.
evidence: This is a statement about the kinetics of photocycle intermediates based on previous characterization.

claim: Previous studies on Channelrhodopsin 1 and 2 (ChR1, ChR2) have revealed an interaction between an aspartate-cysteine (DC) pair localized close to the retinal C13=C14 bond.
source: Previous studies on Channelrhodopsin 1 and 2 (ChR1, ChR2) have revealed an interaction between an aspartate-cysteine (DC) pair localized close to the retinal C13=C14 bond around which photoisomerization occurs.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies on channelrhodopsins.

claim: Disruption of the DC-interaction by mutating the respective residues dramatically slows down the photocycle kinetics in ChR1 and ChR2.
source: Disruption of this DC-interaction by mutating the respective residues dramatically slows down the photocycle kinetics (Ritter et al., 2013; Lórenz-Fonfría and Heberle, 2014; Nack et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ritter et al., 2013; Lórenz-Fonfría and Heberle, 2014; Nack et al., 2010.

claim: A multiple sequence alignment indicated the DC residues to be conserved in CaRGC.
source: A multiple sequence alignment indicated these residues to be conserved in CaRGC, suggesting that a similar mechanism may be exploited to delay its photocycle.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: The C259S mutant of CaRGC decelerated the photocycle about tenfold with seemingly unimpeded functionality.
source: Indeed, as described for ChR1 and ChR2, the C259S mutant of CaRGC decelerated the photocycle about tenfold with seemingly unimpeded functionality.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental characterization of the C259S mutant presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C259S mutant provides an opportunity to study transient photocycle intermediates of CaRGC with the time resolution available with the UV-Vis and FTIR spectroscopic setup.
source: Since FTIR rapid-scan acquisition rates are limited to tenth of milliseconds, the C259S mutant provides an opportunity to study transient photocycle intermediates of CaRGC and their kinetics with the time resolution available with our new UV-Vis and FTIR spectroscopic setup (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic properties of the C259S mutant and the capabilities of the spectroscopic setup.

claim: For single turnover conditions at 20°C, the late L state absorbing at 450 nm precedes the M state absorbing at 350 nm in the C259S mutant.
source: For single turnover conditions at 20°C, the late L state absorbing at 450 nm precedes the M state absorbing at 350 nm.
evidence: This claim is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 20°C under continuous illumination, the slower M state accumulates congruously with no traces of K and L state within the limits of accuracy of the measurement.
source: At the same temperature but under continuous illumination, the slower M state accumulates congruously with no traces of K and L state within the limits of accuracy of the measurement.
evidence: This claim is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At −10°C, the photostationary equilibrium shows clear populations of K, L, and M species favoring the L state.
source: At this temperature, the photostationary equilibrium shows clear populations of K, L, and M species favoring the L state (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In case of single turnover at −10°C, the K state decay becomes visible due to the reduced photocycle kinetics, followed by L state formation.
source: In case of single turnover, the K state decay becomes visible due to the reduced photocycle kinetics, followed by L state formation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At −10°C single turnover, there is no indication for a later population of the M state, although the protein reverts back to the dark state.
source: However, there is no longer an indication for a later population of the M state, although the protein reverts back to the dark state.
evidence: This claim is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data at −10°C single turnover conditions.

claim: The spectral features and decay kinetics at 20°C for single turnover and continuous illumination are similar, implying that the long-lived M intermediate accumulates under continuous illumination.
source: The spectral features and decay kinetics at 20°C for single turnover and continuous illumination are similar, implying that the long-lived M intermediate accumulates under continuous illumination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of FTIR spectra and kinetics shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The steady state spectrum recorded at 20°C represents a nearly pure M state spectrum that is virtually identical for single turnover and steady state illumination.
source: Consequently, the steady state spectrum recorded at 20°C (Figure 1F) represents a nearly pure M state spectrum that is virtually identical for single turnover and steady state illumination (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is based on FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: There is no major branching of the photocycle at room temperature for the C259S mutant.
source: Due to the similar decay kinetics, we exclude a major branching of the photocycle at room temperature (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar decay kinetics observed in the data.

claim: At −10°C, single turnover illumination by short flashes leads to a FTIR difference spectrum that is clearly distinguishable from the spectrum recorded at room temperature and is assigned to the L intermediate.
source: At −10°C, single turnover illumination by short flashes leads to a FTIR difference spectrum that is clearly distinguishable from the spectrum recorded at room temperature. Based on the simultaneously recorded UV-Vis data, we assign this spectrum to the L intermediate.
evidence: This claim is based on FTIR and UV-Vis spectroscopy data at −10°C.

claim: At −10°C under steady state illumination, a global fit analysis of the decay revealed the presence of two distinct spectroscopic components corresponding to L-state and M-state spectra.
source: In case of steady state illumination at −10°, the situation is more complex. After illumination stop, a global fit analysis of the decay revealed the presence of two distinct spectroscopic components (Figure 1J). The upper spectrum (blue line) shows features of the L-state spectrum, whereas the lower one (orange line) shows great congruence with the M state spectrum obtained at room temperature.
evidence: This claim is based on global fit analysis of FTIR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The K state could not be identified in the FTIR data because it is only weakly populated and expected to rapidly decay.
source: As the K state is only weakly populated and expected to rapidly decay, it could not be identified in the FTIR data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected properties of the K state and the limitations of the FTIR method.

claim: Two major bands in the amide I region serve as marker bands for the L and M states (L: 1647(+), M: 1630(+)).
source: These results show the aptitude of two major bands in the amide I region to serve as marker bands for the L and M states (L: 1647(+), M: 1630(+)).
evidence: This claim is based on the FTIR spectroscopy data showing distinct bands for L and M states.

claim: At −10°C, the M state decay is slowed down by only one order of magnitude compared to 20°C.
source: While at −10°C, the M state decay is slowed down by only one order of magnitude compared to 20°C, the L state decay is decelerated by a factor of 50.
evidence: This claim is based on kinetic analysis of the photocycle shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: At −10°C, the L state decay is decelerated by a factor of 50 compared to 20°C.
source: While at −10°C, the M state decay is slowed down by only one order of magnitude compared to 20°C, the L state decay is decelerated by a factor of 50.
evidence: This claim is based on kinetic analysis of the photocycle shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: A L to D relaxation pathway is populated at lower temperatures but not significantly at room temperature.
source: Since the M intermediate could not be identified in the single turnover experiment and is less represented than the L intermediate under continuous illumination at −10°C, we propose a L to D relaxation pathway that is populated at lower temperatures but not significantly at room temperature.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed spectroscopic data at different temperatures.

claim: The presence of two distinct L states, one relaxing back to the dark-adapted state and one leading to M state formation, can be excluded by the identical FTIR L state spectra under continuous and single turnover illumination at −10°C.
source: The presence of two distinct L states, one relaxing back to the dark-adapted state and one leading to M state formation, can be excluded by the identical FTIR L state spectra under continuous and single turnover illumination at −10°C.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of FTIR spectra under different illumination conditions.

claim: The RGC wild type (WT) and RGC C259S spectra show great spectral congruence, indicating that despite the altered reaction kinetics, the structural changes remain nearly unaltered.
source: The RGC wild type (WT) and RGC C259S spectra show great spectral congruence, indicating that despite the altered reaction kinetics, the structural changes remain nearly unaltered.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of FTIR spectra shown in Figure 2.

claim: The full-length RGC and Rh spectra show no obvious qualitative differences and only minor deviations around the amide I and II regions.
source: Similarly, the full-length RGC and Rh spectra show no obvious qualitative differences and only minor deviations around the amide I (1700–1600 cm−1) and II (1590–1510 cm−1) regions.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of FTIR spectra shown in Figure 2.

claim: The changes in the cyclase domain (GC) conformation during light-activation are too small to be identified in the spectra as global structural changes.
source: Thus, we conclude that the changes in the cyclase domain (GC, aa 443–626) conformation during light-activation are too small to be identified in the spectra as global structural changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of obvious differences in FTIR spectra between full-length RGC and Rh.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that the N-terminus plays a crucial role for the catalytic activity of RGCs.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the N-terminus plays a crucial role for the catalytic activity of RGCs, and both C-terminal and N-terminal GC interactions have been proposed (Scheib et al., 2018; Butryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheib et al., 2018 and Butryn et al., 2020.

claim: Both C-terminal and N-terminal GC interactions have been proposed for RGCs.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the N-terminus plays a crucial role for the catalytic activity of RGCs, and both C-terminal and N-terminal GC interactions have been proposed (Scheib et al., 2018; Butryn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheib et al., 2018 and Butryn et al., 2020.

claim: The steady state difference spectra of CaRh with linker domain and complete N-terminus (RhL) and a variant with truncation of the N-terminal residues 1–43 (Rh-43) exhibit no particular differences.
source: Figure 3B shows the steady state difference spectra of CaRh with linker domain and complete N-terminus (RhL, aa 1–442, green line) and a variant with truncation of the N-terminal residues 1–43 (Rh-43, aa 44–396, light green area), without linker domain. The spectra exhibit no particular differences indicating no substantial interaction between the truncated part of the N-terminus and the linker domain or structural changes in the linker domain upon photo-activation.
evidence: This claim is based on FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Truncation of N-terminal residues 1–43 does not impede the catalytic activity of RGC but rather increases it.
source: Our observation is in accordance with the previous finding that this truncation does not impede the catalytic activity of RGC but rather increases it (Scheib, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib, 2019.

claim: The Rh-139 variant shows smaller structural differences compared to Rh-43 as concluded from the altered amide I and II regions.
source: Compared to Rh-43 (light red area), the overall absorption pattern remains almost unchanged. The presence of the 1630(+) band in both spectra indicates accumulation of the M state at 4°C in both variants. However, smaller structural differences occur in the Rh-139 variant as concluded from the altered amide I and II regions.
evidence: This claim is based on FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 1630(+) band indicates accumulation of the M state at 4°C in both Rh-43 and Rh-139 variants.
source: The presence of the 1630(+) band in both spectra indicates accumulation of the M state at 4°C in both variants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photo-induced structural alterations in the N-terminus or Rh domain occur due to truncation of the residues 43–139.
source: This data provides evidence for photo-induced structural alterations in the N-terminus or Rh domain due to truncation of the residues 43–139.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences observed in FTIR spectra between Rh-43 and Rh-139.

claim: The cytosolic N-terminus is involved in the photo-induced structural rearrangements of RGC that may support signal propagation from the Rh to the GC domain.
source: It indicates an involvement of the cytosolic N-terminus in the photo-induced structural rearrangements of RGC that may support signal propagation from the Rh to the GC domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FTIR spectroscopy data of truncated variants.

claim: The RGC-139 variant shows complete absence of enzymatic activity.
source: This is supported by the complete absence of enzymatic activity in the RGC-139 variant (Scheib, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib, 2019.

claim: The RGCs enzymatic functionality has been successfully demonstrated upon coexpression with cGMP-selective CNG-A2 channels in Xenopus oocytes and hippocampal neurons.
source: The RGCs enzymatic functionality has been successfully demonstrated upon coexpression with cGMP-selective CNG-A2 channels in Xenopus oocytes and hippocampal neurons (Scheib et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheib et al., 2015 and Gao et al., 2015.

claim: Protein of all samples was tested via an HPLC assay which demonstrated the necessity to use a photolabile caged GTP substitute which is not turned over by the RGC dark activity.
source: To verify enzymatic activity, protein of all samples was also tested via an HPLC assay (Appendix 6) which demonstrated on the one hand the necessity to use a photolabile caged GTP substitute which is not turned over by the RGC dark activity and on the other hand, that cGMP is successfully produced by free GC when illuminating the caged NPE-GTP compound with UV-light.
evidence: This claim is based on HPLC assay data presented in Appendix 6.

claim: cGMP is successfully produced by free GC when illuminating the caged NPE-GTP compound with UV-light.
source: To verify enzymatic activity, protein of all samples was also tested via an HPLC assay (Appendix 6) which demonstrated on the one hand the necessity to use a photolabile caged GTP substitute which is not turned over by the RGC dark activity and on the other hand, that cGMP is successfully produced by free GC when illuminating the caged NPE-GTP compound with UV-light.
evidence: This claim is based on HPLC assay data presented in Appendix 6.

claim: NPE-GTP binds to the RGC moiety prior to UV illumination.
source: Therefore, we conclude that NPE-GTP binds to the RGC moiety prior to UV illumination, thus avoiding major phosphate rearrangements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FTIR spectroscopy data showing altered phosphate bands in NPE-GTP·RGC compared to free NPE-GTP.

claim: The interaction between the guanine group and E497 exists already in the dark and remains unchanged upon illumination.
source: Obviously, the interaction between the guanine group and E497 (Figure 4B) exists already in the dark and remains unchanged upon illumination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of spectral changes in the carboxylic region >1690 cm−1 in the FTIR data.

claim: The 1117(-) to 1070(+) down shift may be interpreted as a weakening of the P=O vibrations due to slight reorientation of the α- and β-phosphates in the binding pocket after uncaging.
source: The 1117(-) to 1070(+) down shift may be interpreted as a weakening of the P=O vibrations due to slight reorientation of the α- and β-phosphates in the binding pocket after uncaging.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data.

claim: The 1529(-), 1198(-), and 1186(-) bands indicate retinal isomerization.
source: Most strikingly, the 1529(-), 1198(-), and 1186(-) bands indicate retinal isomerization, while the 1630(+) band marks the formation and accumulation of the M state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data based on known vibrational modes of retinal.

claim: The 1630(+) band marks the formation and accumulation of the M state.
source: Most strikingly, the 1529(-), 1198(-), and 1186(-) bands indicate retinal isomerization, while the 1630(+) band marks the formation and accumulation of the M state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data based on previous assignment of the M state marker band.

claim: The strong positive 1087(+) and 1068(+) bands represent the P=O vibrations arising with the formation of the cGMP.
source: This applies to the strong positive 1087(+) and 1068(+) bands, representing the P=O vibrations arising with the formation of the cGMP. This assignment is based on the great congruence with the cGMP absolute spectrum shaded in light red.
evidence: This assignment is based on comparison with the cGMP absolute spectrum shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 1068 band is unique to the cGMP spectrum and is assigned to the cyclic phosphate bond.
source: As seen in direct comparison, only the 1068 band is unique to the cGMP spectrum, allowing an assignment to the cyclic phosphate bond.
evidence: This assignment is based on comparison of absolute spectra of GTP, cGMP, and PP shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The rapid rise of the 1087(+) vibration after illumination onset reflects the high initial cGMP production.
source: After illumination onset, the rapid rise of the 1087(+) vibration (Figure 4E, red line) reflects the high initial cGMP production, which then levels out to a reduced but constant slope.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic trace shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The instantaneous cGMP production upon formation of the M-state is visualized by almost identical kinetics of the M-state vibration at 1630(+) and the cGMP vibration at 1087(+) during illumination onset.
source: The instantaneous cGMP production upon formation of the M-state is visualized by almost identical kinetics of the M-state vibration at 1630(+) and the cGMP vibration at 1087(+) during illumination onset, which are shown as inset in Figure 4E.
evidence: This claim is based on the kinetic traces shown in the inset of Figure 4E.

claim: A substantial dark activity exists before and after RGC light-activation.
source: The grey lines, which are fitted to the kinetic sections of approximately constant slope, reveal a substantial dark activity before and after RGC light-activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic traces shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The cleavage of the phosphodiester bond between α- and β-phosphate associated with GTP to cGMP conversion is reflected by the negative 1244(-) and 1155(-) bands.
source: The cleavage of the phosphodiester bond between α- and β-phosphate associated with GTP to cGMP conversion is reflected by the negative 1244(-) and 1155(-) bands (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After light-off, rhodopsin inactivation is indicated by the disappearance of the prominent Rh bands above 1400 cm−1 and 1630 M-state marker band.
source: After light-off, rhodopsin inactivation is indicated by the disappearance of the prominent Rh bands above 1400 cm−1 (Figure 4D, violet line) and 1630 M-state marker band kinetic shown in Figure 4E (orange line).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The negative 923(-) band gains intensity upon cGMP release and is assigned to the GTP P-O-P vibration.
source: Moreover, the negative 923(-) band gains intensity upon cGMP release. The absence of absorption bands in the cGMP and PP absolute spectra allows an assignment to the GTP P-O-P vibration (see Figure 5A), leading to a reduced absorbance over time whilst the GTP is turned over.
evidence: This assignment is based on comparison with absolute spectra shown in Figure 5A and the kinetic behavior.

claim: The NPE-GTP was almost completely bound to the GC protein prior to cleavage.
source: Especially the negative band at 1256 cm−1 associated with the γ-phosphate PO2- stretching vibration appears to be displaced at 1207 cm−1, indicating that also in this sample the NPE-GTP was almost completely bound to the protein prior to cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the displacement of the γ-phosphate band in the FTIR spectrum shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The PO32- stretching vibration, formed upon photolysis, appears upshifted to 1132 cm−1 in GC·NPE-GTP.
source: The PO32- stretching vibration, formed upon photolysis, which was found at 1122 cm−1 for free GTP (Cepus et al., 1998b), appears upshifted to 1132 cm−1.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the free GTP spectrum and a citation to Cepus et al., 1998b.

claim: Similar shifts of the PO32- stretching vibration were observed for Ras bound NPE-GTP upon uncaging.
source: Similar shifts were observed for Ras bound NPE-GTP upon uncaging (Cepus et al., 1998a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cepus et al., 1998a.

claim: The 1087 and 1122 band kinetics show the instantaneous GTP uncaging as a step followed by cGMP production and simultaneous GTP disappearance.
source: The 1087 and 1122 band kinetics depicted in Figure 4G show the instantaneous GTP uncaging as a step. This is then followed by cGMP production, as the 1087 band rises and simultaneous GTP disappearance as is indicated by the decline of the 1122 band.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic traces shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The enzymatic process in GC was found to already be saturated during the measurement.
source: The enzymatic process was found to already be saturated during the measurement.
evidence: This is an observation based on the kinetic behavior shown in Figure 4G.

claim: An experiment with 10 times higher NPE-GTP concentration shows that the reaction kinetic and its saturation are accelerated, suggesting feedback inhibition by the reaction product cGMP.
source: An analog experiment with 10 times higher NPE-GTP concentration (Figure 4G inset) shows that the reaction kinetic and its saturation are accelerated, suggesting feedback inhibition by the reaction product cGMP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data shown in the inset of Figure 4G.

claim: The positive 1267(+) band is assigned to the UV-light-induced release of the NAP-group.
source: Since the same band originates in the photolysis spectrum of the GTP analog NPE-GPCPP (Appendix 2), we assigned this band to the UV-light-induced release of the NAP-group.
evidence: This assignment is based on comparison with the NPE-GPCPP photolysis spectrum shown in Appendix 2.

claim: Differences in the phosphate region in the GTP·RGC complex compared to the GTP·GC complex reflect differences of GTP binding to an inactive and an active cyclase domain.
source: Differences in the phosphate region in the GTP·RGC complex between 1300 and 1000 cm−1 compared to those in the spectrum of the GTP·GC complex reflect differences of GTP binding to an inactive (Figure 4D, blue line) and an active cyclase domain (Figure 4F, blue line).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences observed in FTIR spectra between inactive RGC and active GC.

claim: The photolysis spectrum of RGC upon UV-uncaging of NPE-ATP shows an overall congruence with a photolysis spectrum acquired for uncaging of free NPE-ATP in solution.
source: The photolysis spectrum (blue line) shows an overall congruence with a photolysis spectrum acquired for uncaging of free NPE-ATP in solution despite the reduced signal quality.
evidence: This is based on comparison of FTIR spectra shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Caged ATP is unable to form tight bonding to the dark-adapted RGC active site, unlike caged GTP.
source: This observation hints towards a caged ATP, which is, unlike caged GTP, unable to form tight bonding to the dark-adapted RGC active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of the NPE-ATP photolysis spectrum with free NPE-ATP.

claim: A different binding mode of NPE-ATP to RGC, that in contrast to GTP is unable to interact tightly with E497 and C566, is indicated.
source: A different binding mode of NPE-ATP to RGC, that in contrast to GTP is unable to interact tightly with E497 and C566, is further indicated as no shift of the negative 1256 band is observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of band shift in the FTIR spectrum shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The NPE-group impairs the correct orchestration of the phosphate chain effectively inhibiting substrate retention in the active site.
source: Additionally, the NPE-group impairs the correct orchestration of the phosphate chain effectively inhibiting substrate retention in the active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FTIR spectroscopy data of NPE-ATP binding.

claim: Flash photolysis experiments on CaRh WT showed a sequential photoreaction at room temperature.
source: In accordance with our findings, flash photolysis experiments on CaRh WT showed a sequential photoreaction at room temperature (Scheib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2018.

claim: The M state spectra of the C259S mutant and the WT do not exhibit any obvious differences.
source: Interestingly, the M state spectra of the mutant and the WT (Figure 2) do not exhibit any obvious differences which might hint towards the causal root of the deceleration.
evidence: This is based on comparison of FTIR spectra shown in Figure 2.

claim: No clear evidence for the population of parallel photocycles starting from 13-trans, 15-anti or 13-cis, 15-syn retinal was found for CaRGC.
source: Despite the clustering of common features, no clear evidence for the population of parallel photocycles starting from 13-trans, 15-anti or 13-cis, 15-syn retinal was found for CaRGC as reported for ChR2 (Kuhne et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the spectroscopic data and comparison with ChR2.

claim: The L-state FTIR difference spectrum is dominated by a 1665 (-)/1647(+) cm−1 double band which suggests hydration of a transmembrane α-helix within the Rh moiety due to water influx.
source: The L-state FTIR difference spectrum (see Appendix 3) is dominated by a 1665 (-)/1647(+) cm−1 double band which suggests hydration of a transmembrane α-helix within the Rh moiety due to water influx, as proposed for Channelrhodopsin (Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectrum based on comparison with Channelrhodopsin and supported by a citation to Lórenz-Fonfría et al., 2015.

claim: The FTIR difference spectra of the M-intermediate show prominent bands at 1622, 1630 and 1677, 1688 cm−1 indicating conformational changes that may be interpreted as formation of new β-sheet structures in the rhodopsin domain.
source: In CaRGC, the FTIR difference spectra of the M-intermediate show prominent bands at 1622, 1630 and 1677, 1688 cm−1 indicating conformational changes that may be interpreted as formation of new β-sheet structures in the rhodopsin domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FTIR spectroscopy data.

claim: At least at low temperatures, the recovery of the RGC dark state proceeds directly from L via a second relaxation pathway (short cut).
source: Besides confirming a classical sequential photocycle involving an M-state with deprotonated RSB, our experiments showed that, at least at low temperatures, the recovery of the RGC dark state also proceeds directly from L via a second relaxation pathway (short cut).
evidence: This is based on the spectroscopic data at low temperatures showing L state decay without M state formation.

claim: Both L-state decay paths have comparable rate constants at −10°C, indicating a metastable L-state.
source: Based on our FTIR data, both L-state decay paths, either directly back to the dark state or via the M-state, have comparable rate constants at −10°C, indicating a metastable L-state.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of the FTIR data at −10°C.

claim: The M-state is thermodynamically more stable than the L-state and thus better suited to trigger enzyme activation.
source: In contrast, the putative β-sheet conformation in the M-state is thermodynamically more stable and thus better suited to trigger enzyme activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic and spectroscopic properties of the M-state.

claim: The M-state was proposed as the catalytically active state of RGC.
source: While the M-state was proposed as the catalytically active state of RGC (Scheib et al., 2018), our FTIR study confirmed this assumption by revealing a direct correlation of the M-state and cGMP formation indicated by the kinetics of the respective marker bands at 1630 cm−1 (M) and 1087 cm−1 (cGMP).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2018 and confirmed by the FTIR data in this study.

claim: FTIR difference spectroscopy assigns the vast majority of the structural rearrangements occurring after photoactivation to the rhodopsin domain.
source: Remarkably, FTIR difference spectroscopy assigns the vast majority of the structural rearrangements occurring after photoactivation to the rhodopsin domain, while the contributions of linker and GC domain to the spectral features are marginal.
evidence: This is a summary of the FTIR spectroscopy findings.

claim: In soluble NO sensing GC (sGC), NO binding induces major conformational changes.
source: For example, in soluble NO sensing GC (sGC), NO binding induces major conformational changes (Kang et al., 2019), whereas the structural alterations in a soluble light-activated adenylyl cyclase from cyanobacteria upon activation are minor and therefore difficult to track (Ohki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kang et al., 2019.

claim: The structural alterations in a soluble light-activated adenylyl cyclase from cyanobacteria upon activation are minor and therefore difficult to track.
source: For example, in soluble NO sensing GC (sGC), NO binding induces major conformational changes (Kang et al., 2019), whereas the structural alterations in a soluble light-activated adenylyl cyclase from cyanobacteria upon activation are minor and therefore difficult to track (Ohki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ohki et al., 2017.

claim: The GC dimer activity is regulated by a small angular repositioning of the two subunits towards one another that leaves their internal structure and overall peptide environment nearly undisturbed.
source: Previous studies on type III cyclases report the GC dimer activity to be regulated by a small angular repositioning of the two subunits towards one another that leaves their internal structure and overall peptide environment nearly undisturbed (Butryn et al., 2020; Krissinel and Henrick, 2007; Steegborn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butryn et al., 2020; Krissinel and Henrick, 2007; Steegborn, 2014.

claim: A slight rotation of TM7 could propagate through the linker and affect the GC domain in analogy to the sensory rhodopsin II signaling pathway.
source: Accordingly, a slight rotation of TM7 could propagate through the linker and affect the GC domain in analogy to the sensory rhodopsin II signaling pathway (Gordeliy et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on analogy with sensory rhodopsin II and supported by a citation to Gordeliy et al., 2002.

claim: Light-induced structural changes in the M state involve the N-terminal residues 44–139.
source: Our data shows, however, light-induced structural changes in the M state that involve the N-terminal residues 44–139.
evidence: This is based on the FTIR spectroscopy data of truncated variants.

claim: Removal of the cytosolic N-terminus (RGC-139) results in the complete loss of enzymatic function.
source: Since removal of the cytosolic N-terminus (RGC-139) results in the complete loss of enzymatic function (Scheib, 2019), the linker contact has to hold the GC domain in an catalytic inactive position.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib, 2019.

claim: The linker contact holds the GC domain in a catalytically inactive position.
source: Since removal of the cytosolic N-terminus (RGC-139) results in the complete loss of enzymatic function (Scheib, 2019), the linker contact has to hold the GC domain in an catalytic inactive position.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of activity upon N-terminus removal.

claim: The N-terminus mediates the activation by either releasing the inhibitory linker contact or by directly altering the GC conformation.
source: Consequently, the N-terminus mediates the activation by either releasing the inhibitory linker contact or by directly altering the GC conformation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the functional data.

claim: Light-activated RGC is more active than free GC alone.
source: Since it has been shown that light-activated RGC is more active than free GC alone we presume the latter (Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mukherjee et al., 2019.

claim: The N-terminal rearrangement in the M state introduces small but crucial modifications of the active site as a requirement for cyclase activation.
source: As our results suggest, the N-terminal rearrangement in the M state introduces small but crucial modifications of the active site as a requirement for cyclase activation (Scheib et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2017; Alben et al., 1974).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectroscopic data and supported by citations to Scheib et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2017; Alben et al., 1974.

claim: Highly conserved linker constructs are involved in GC and AC regulation.
source: Since highly conserved linker constructs are involved in GC and AC regulation (Ma et al., 2010; Vercellino et al., 2017; Ziegler et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2019; Khannpnavar et al., 2020; Seth et al., 2020), a similar mechanism cannot be disregarded to play a role in RGCs as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on GC and AC regulation.

claim: The CaRGC transducer element is predicted to form a structural motif consisting of an elongated TM and a short handle helix which is most similar to the S-helical domains found for example in Gsα.
source: The CaRGC transducer element is predicted to form a structural motif consisting of an elongated TM and a short handle helix which is most similar to the S-helical domains found for example in Gsα.
evidence: This is a structural prediction based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Signal propagation presumably requires a concerted reorientation of both, linker domain and N-terminus.
source: Therefore, signal propagation presumably requires a concerted reorientation of both, linker domain and N-terminus.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Photo-activation does not regulate the accessibility of the binding site in RGC.
source: They disclosed that NPE-GTP already binds to the dark-adapted RGC catalytic site, ruling out that photo-activation regulates the accessibility of the binding site as discussed for other type III cyclases (e.g. sGC) (Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NPE-GTP binds to dark-adapted RGC.

claim: Base interactions are involved in substrate binding to RGC.
source: Analogous experiments with NPE-ATP show lower binding of caged ATP to the protein compared to GTP, suggesting that base interactions are involved in substrate binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential binding of NPE-ATP and NPE-GTP.

claim: Base-binding has been assigned to occur rather late during catalytic turnover in type III cyclases.
source: This is remarkable, because so far, base-binding has been assigned to occur rather late during catalytic turnover, whereas substrate binding was considered to be dominated by the protein-metal-phosphate interaction (Steegborn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steegborn, 2014.

claim: Substrate binding in type III cyclases was considered to be dominated by the protein-metal-phosphate interaction.
source: This is remarkable, because so far, base-binding has been assigned to occur rather late during catalytic turnover, whereas substrate binding was considered to be dominated by the protein-metal-phosphate interaction (Steegborn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steegborn, 2014.

claim: RGC is able to bind GTP in the dark state without the need to open and close the active site.
source: The fact that RGC is able to bind GTP in the dark state without the need to open and close the active site, is consistent with our observation that little structural rearrangement of GC occurs upon photoactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate binding data and the lack of major structural changes in GC upon photoactivation.

claim: The main regulation of catalytic function in RGC takes place in the active site.
source: The main regulation of catalytic function seems to take place in the active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate binding and spectroscopic data.

claim: The presence of the dark-adapted Rh domain prevents vibrational uncoupling of the phosphate vibrations.
source: In the isolated GC, well-separated phosphate bands were observed in contrast to the broader bands in the inactive RGC, thus indicating that the presence of the dark-adapted Rh domain prevents vibrational uncoupling of the phosphate vibrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in phosphate bands between GC and dark-adapted RGC.

claim: Vibrational uncoupling of phosphate vibrations has been observed for Ras bound GTP as a prerequisite of phosphate chain cleavage.
source: This uncoupling has been observed for Ras bound GTP as a prerequisite of phosphate chain cleavage (Allin et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Allin et al., 2001.

claim: RGC shows substantial dark activity in detergent which does not exist for RGC in host membranes.
source: The experiments also revealed a substantial RGC dark activity in detergent which does not exist for RGC in host membranes and necessitates the use of caged GTP compounds.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data.

claim: The RGC dark activity in detergent may be caused by the residual presence of free GC due to unspecific fragmentation during protein preparation or the high protein concentration in detergent.
source: This may be caused by the residual presence of free GC due to unspecific fragmentation during protein preparation or the high protein concentration in detergent.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed dark activity.

claim: The NPE-caging group located at the γ-phosphate modifies the binding site but does not prevent its occupation.
source: The NPE-caging group located at the γ-phosphate modifies the binding site but does not prevent its occupation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate binding data.

claim: The NPE-caging group impedes correct orchestration of the phosphate chain, effectively disabling the formation of the transition state leading to the cleavage of the α-β phosphate bond.
source: Instead, it impedes correct orchestration of the phosphate chain, effectively disabling the formation of the transition state leading to the cleavage of the α-β phosphate bond.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of substrate turnover with caged substrates in the dark.

claim: GTP preincubation was found to be an experimental requirement since substrate diffusion into the binding site is insufficient in the highly concentrated detergent samples necessary for FTIR transmission spectroscopy.
source: GTP preincubation was found to be an experimental requirement since substrate diffusion into the binding site is insufficient in the highly concentrated detergent samples necessary for FTIR transmission spectroscopy.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental conditions.

claim: The purine-base discriminating interaction assigned to the residues C566 and E497 are indispensable for catalysis.
source: As expected, no substrate turnover was observed in experiments with NPE-ATP, indicating that the purine-base discriminating interaction assigned to the residues C566 and E497 are indispensable for catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of turnover with NPE-ATP.

claim: Two metal ions, A and B, are involved in the catalysis of type III cyclases, believed to be Mg2+ under physiological conditions in most type III cyclases.
source: As deduced from various functional and structural studies, two metal ions, A and B (Figure 6), are involved in the catalysis, believed to be Mg2+ under physiological conditions in most type III cyclases (Steegborn, 2014; Tesmer et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steegborn, 2014 and Tesmer et al., 1999.

claim: Ion B is permanently present and mediates binding of the phosphate moiety of the substrate.
source: While ion B is permanently present and mediates binding of the phosphate moiety of the substrate, ion A resides only temporary and may tune the electrostatic environment of the ribose-3'OH for the nucleophilic attack of the α-phosphate.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional studies of type III cyclases.

claim: Ion A resides only temporarily and may tune the electrostatic environment of the ribose-3'OH for the nucleophilic attack of the α-phosphate.
source: While ion B is permanently present and mediates binding of the phosphate moiety of the substrate, ion A resides only temporary and may tune the electrostatic environment of the ribose-3'OH for the nucleophilic attack of the α-phosphate.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional studies of type III cyclases.

claim: Both monomers are involved in GTP/ATP binding with the purine-base and the phosphates interacting with different monomers.
source: Notably, both monomers are involved in GTP/ATP binding with the purine-base and the phosphates interacting with different monomers; thus, slight changes of the dimeric arrangement during protein closure may trigger the conformation of the substrate to allow cyclization.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of type III cyclases.

claim: Most type III cyclases have remarkable substrate specificity, catalyzing either ATP or GTP.
source: Most type III cyclases have remarkable substrate specificity, catalyzing either ATP or GTP, rendering precise nucleotide base orientation crucial.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type III cyclases.

claim: An activation mechanism involving structural reorientation of the β4/5 loop immediately preceding the nucleotide base-contacting β5 region of the cyclase domain has been proposed.
source: Therefore, the interaction of the protein to the purine holds the potential to regulate cyclase activity. Accordingly, an activation mechanism involving structural reorientation of the β4/5 loop immediately preceding the nucleotide base-contacting β5 region of the cyclase domain has been proposed. This mechanism derived originally from the analysis of various crystal structures of a soluble light-activated adenylyl cyclase from the bacterium Beggiatoa sp. (Lindner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lindner et al., 2017.

claim: Different conformations of the β4/5 loop have been reported for the crystal structure of a CaGC mutant.
source: Different conformations of this flexible loop have also been reported for the crystal structure of a CaGC mutant (Scheib et al., 2018), providing some evidence that this region may also be involved in enzyme activation in CaRGC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheib et al., 2018.

claim: A certain amount of flexibility in the positioning of the residue R577 on helix α4 after β5 has been reported, which might indicate a regulatory role in conjunction with the proposed purine-base interaction.
source: The same study reported a certain amount of flexibility in the positioning of the residue R577 on helix α4 after β5 (Appendix 5—figure 1B) which might indicate a regulatory role in conjunction with the proposed purine-base interaction.
evidence: This is based on structural data from a previous study.

claim: The positive charge of R577 is discussed to compensate the temporary additional negative charge at the pentavalent α-phosphate during cyclization.
source: The positive charge of R577 is discussed to compensate the temporary additional negative charge at the pentavalent α-phosphate during cyclization (Steegborn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steegborn, 2014.

claim: The potential impact of positive charged residues on hydrolysis of GTP has been described in detail for the GTPase reaction of H-Ras P21, which produces GDP and Pi.
source: The potential impact of positive charged residues on hydrolysis of GTP has been described in detail for the GTPase reaction of H-Ras P21, which produces GDP and Pi (Cepus et al., 1998b; Allin and Gerwert, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cepus et al., 1998b and Allin and Gerwert, 2001.

claim: Binding of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) places a single arginine residue close to the β-phosphate group thereby accelerating the GTP hydrolysis rate by five orders of magnitude.
source: Binding of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) places a single arginine residue close to the β-phosphate group thereby accelerating the GTP hydrolysis rate by five orders of magnitude Allin et al., 2001; Rudack et al., 2012.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allin et al., 2001 and Rudack et al., 2012.

claim: Fungal RGCs have been described that function as obligate heterodimers, which utilize only one of the rhodopsin domains for direct light-activation.
source: Only recently, fungal RGCs have been described that function as obligate heterodimers, which utilizes only one of the rhodopsin domains for direct light-activation Broser et al., 2020.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Broser et al., 2020.

claim: The light-activated rhodopsin-cyclase subunit of heterodimeric RGCs shares up to ∼45% sequence identity with CaRGC but is completely inactive as homodimer.
source: This light-activated rhodopsin-cyclase subunit shares up to ∼45% sequence identity with CaRGC but is completely inactive as homodimer.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and functional data from the cited study.

claim: The N-terminus of the light-activated rhodopsin-cyclase subunit of heterodimeric RGCs is ∼80 aa shorter compared to CaRGC and particularly the region aa 43–139 of CaRGC is barely conserved.
source: Notably, the N-terminus of this rhodopsin is ∼80 aa shorter compared to CaRGC and particularly the region aa 43–139 of CaRGC is barely conserved, providing further evidence for a functional role of this region in homodimeric CaRGC.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and provides supporting evidence for the functional role of the N-terminus.
